about.label: 01 / ABOUT
about.heading: Hi, I'm Minh Anh
copy: I am interested in how data and technology can help us better understand human health. This interest arose from the desire to find evidence-based solutions for challenges that those around me and I face.

Through leading The Mindful Odyssey, a well-being initiative—and VTEC, my school's technology club, I have learned to approach problems with curiosity, responsibility, and a willingness to revise my ideas when they fall short.

I hope to strengthen my skills in mathematics, programming, and statistical analysis as well as communication, critical thinking, and interdisciplinary understanding. Ultimately, I want to learn to ask better questions, communicate clearly, and design solutions around people's actual needs.

copy: For my first research project, I surveyed students across my school and ran an eight-week pilot program on a mindfulness-based group intervention. The study examines sleep patterns and explores whether weekly mindfulness practice may be associated with changes in self-reported sleep.

popups.title: Slumbering

image.alt: Four Slumbering app screens: home with tonight's goals and badges, the Journey log, bedtime and wake-up charts, and sleep sounds

popups.roleDates: Designed and built independently with AI assistance, Jun-Aug 2026

rows.label: Why
rows.text: Many students are aware of healthy sleep habits but struggle to maintain them consistently. I wanted to design a tool that makes small changes easier, without the guilt of missing a goal.

rows.label: What it does
rows.list: An Android app in Vietnamese · Set small nightly goals for bedtime, winding down, or relaxation · Check in each morning · Track streaks and recent nights on the Journey screen · Earn seven badges · View bedtime charts · Play eight sleep sounds · Set three reminders · Keep all data on the device

rows.label: Design choices
rows.list: A missed goal counts as feedback for the next night · Sound files download on first use to keep the app small · After feedback raised questions about the scientific basis and the number of features, I simplified the first version · Each feature has its own screen, and a short onboarding makes the app easier to understand

rows.label: Results
rows.list: Shared publicly and updated in response to user feedback · Tried by several BewellNest members and other students

rows.label: Skills
rows.list: Designing for a specific user group · Simplifying features from feedback · App development with AI assistance · Publishing a release

rows.label: Lesson
rows.text: A smaller set of clearly explained features can be more useful than a crowded app.

popups.title: DS-in-the-making

image.alt: SHAP chart ranking the features most linked to insomnia in a public sleep and lifestyle dataset

popups.roleDates: Self-directed projects with AI assistance, Jun 2026-present

rows.label: Why
rows.text: Before analyzing my own survey data, I wanted to practice connecting everyday habits with health-related outcomes using public datasets.

items.did: Trained a Random Forest classifier to predict obesity level and evaluated it with five-fold cross-validation
Used SHAP with a Random Forest classifier to examine features linked to insomnia and sleep apnea
items.result: A ranked chart of the most influential features

items.did: Modeled how pre-bedtime screen time relates to REM sleep
items.result: A broad negative trend, but not reliable for individual predictions

items.did: Used t-tests to explore whether a blue-light filter was linked to less next-day fatigue among high-brightness phone users
items.result: A line chart comparing fatigue with the filter on and off

items.did: Compared XGBoost and Random Forest models for predicting next-day fatigue
items.result: The XGBoost model reached R² ≈ 0.83, explaining about 83% of the variation in next-day fatigue in this dataset

rows.label: Skills
rows.list: Data cleaning · Classification and regression models · Cross-validation · Explaining models with SHAP · t-tests

rows.label: Lesson
rows.text: Public datasets often arrive tidy. Real survey responses need much more careful cleaning.

rows.label: Vision
rows.text: A lightweight reminder tool appears as a desktop pet. It is noticeable enough to prompt action and friendly enough not to feel intrusive.

rows.label: What it does
rows.list: A pixel-art cat or dog appears on a Windows desktop with a speech bubble · Customize pets and reminder categories · Set rules for each reminder, including its message, frequency, and active days · Choose OK or Snooze to dismiss or delay a reminder · Runs in the background while keeping all data on the computer

rows.label: Design aim
rows.text: Make reminders pleasant to notice, so taking action feels easier.

rows.label: Results
rows.text: Used daily by my friends and me to manage our reminders.

rows.label: Skills
rows.list: User-focused design · Customizable reminder logic · Desktop app development with AI assistance

rows.label: Lesson
rows.text: A simple tool can be useful when it addresses a specific, everyday problem.

rows.text: I wanted to explore a practical use for real-time hand tracking.

rows.text: A webcam tracks hand movements and maps selected gestures to keyboard inputs, letting users play games such as Subway Surfers without touching the keyboard.

rows.list: Python · OpenCV for the camera feed and image processing · MediaPipe for hand tracking · PyAutoGUI to send keyboard inputs

popups.title: How well do students sleep, and what role might mindfulness play?

image.alt: Distribution of sleep quality scores among surveyed students (N = 343)

rows.label: Research topic
rows.text: Sleep quality in middle and high school students and the potential of mindfulness-based group intervention

rows.label: My role
rows.text: Researcher, working with one teammate under the supervision of the School Psychology Office

rows.label: Context
rows.list: Sleep quality covers how well a person falls asleep, stays asleep, wakes up, and feels rested. · Biological changes during puberty shift the body toward a later bedtime, which—combined with early school start times, homework, and the use of electronic devices—interferes with getting sufficient sleep. · Poor sleep in students is linked with weaker attention, lower mood, and lower academic performance. · Mindfulness practices have been shown to improve sleep quality, but there is relatively little research on their application in school settings. · Most existing research uses older teens or university students, and relatively little uses Vietnamese school-aged samples.

rows.label: Purpose
rows.list: Describe the self-reported sleep quality of middle and high school students at Vinschool Times City from a behavioral perspective · Compare self-reported sleep quality by grade and gender · Examine the impact of behavioral patterns on self-reported sleep · Explore whether weekly mindfulness group sessions (BewellNest) may link to changes in self-reported sleep

rows.label: Methodology
rows.steps: 1. Reviewed existing studies to identify a research gap and wrote proposal and protocol · 2. Prepared the questionnaire (adapted from the Adolescent Sleep-Wake Scale), consent form and assent form · 3. Surveyed 581 students, combining convenient sampling and random sampling · 4. Ran an eight-week pilot with around 20 BewellNest members · 5. Cleaned and described the data; compared patterns by subscale, grade level, and gender.

rows.label: Results
rows.list: 581 students participated in the survey, 343 were considered (116 male, 216 female, 11 other). The mean age was 13.77 years (SD = 1.88). · The overall sleep quality score was M = 3.94 (SD = 0.74) on a 1 to 6 scale, and the weakest subscale was Waking up. · Self-reported sleep quality did not show significant differences between grade levels. · The difference in overall sleep quality between males and females was significant, t(236.52) = 2.79, p = .006, with a small-to-medium effect (Hedges’ g = 0.32). Males reported better sleep quality. · The time it took to fall asleep had the strongest negative correlation with overall sleep quality.

rows.label: Note
rows.text: Pilot analysis in progress. Final paper is due Nov 20.

rows.label: Implications
rows.list: Schools could use a short screening tool to spot students at risk, especially on the weakest subscale. · Measures to improve sleep may focus on sleep hygiene to decrease the time it takes to fall asleep. · Students' self-reported sleep quality may not be consistent with clinical sleep quality. · The findings give a baseline for later sleep programs, including the mindfulness pilot. · The findings add local data on Vietnamese adolescents' sleep.

rows.label: Limitations
rows.list: The data are self-reported, so answers may be biased. · The design is cross-sectional, so it shows differences at one point in time and cannot show cause. · The sample came from one school and volunteers, so results may not generalize. · The gender groups were unequal in size, and the “other” group (n = 11) was too small to analyze. · Results are mostly descriptive, and there was no comparison group.

rows.label: Future research questions
rows.list: Which factors explain the difference in sleep quality across individuals? · How does sleep quality change across grades and over a school year? · Do the findings hold in other schools and regions of Vietnam?

rows.label: Learned
rows.list: Research-question development · Study design · Consent and assent procedures · Data cleaning · Descriptive and inferential statistics
